doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

title: Disneyland, Joe Darensbourg and George Probert: hearing the Creole clarinet sound
summary: At Disneyland he first heard Joe Darensbourg's Creole sound, distinct from swing clarinet. George Probert gave him recordings, and this contrast underlies why he advocates New Orleans music over Dixieland.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: actually just came up out of the ground and so the parade had its own soundtrack. But in the interim, before they got ready for the parade they played some music of some musicians that used to be at Disneyland and one of them was a Louisiana clarinetist. He wasn’t New Orleans, in fact it was Baton Rouge, but he worked with Kid Ory. His name was Joe Darensbourg. And he ended up on the west coast. And Joe had a wonderful kind of Creole sound on his clarinet and it was I remember one of the first times I remember being very conscious that this is different than like Benny Goodman or Artie Shaw or any of the Swing Era clarinet players that I loved so much. And it really tickled me. And it was probably about that time that I was getting to know George Probert, who worked with the original Firehouse Five Plus Two. And he played clarinet with Kid Ory too, clarinet and soprano sax. And George gave me a lot of recordings of New Orleans cats and everything like that. So I’ll say for that reason also, just my personal experience of working in California, I recognize that there is a huge difference between Dixieland and New Orleans music. And when I really began to try to appreciate how New Orleans music is connected to the culture of the city, the cultural life of the city, and how the more commercial side of it resembled what I did as a young musician in California resembled what musicians in New Orleans did maybe for the tourists. You understand what I’m saying?

I’m not saying that one is completely devoid of commercialness, and I’m not saying that the other is completely devoid of being culturally relevant. I’m not saying that either. I’m just saying that if they fall on one side or another, I’d rather — I feel that I can be a stronger advocate for the traditions if I’m framing them in the context of it being something that’s historically, socially and culturally important rather than framing it as in a novelty offshoot or a throwback from, not to be considered on the same level as the artistic jazz tradition. So that’s why I intentionally — that’s the very long version of why I don’t use the word Dixieland.
